core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Bronchial Asthma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Review and demonstrate correct MDI inhaler technique (with or without spacer), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: wheezing and shortness of breath when exercising

Key HPI features: mild wheezing and dry cough after running outdoors, especially in cold air. Occurs 2-3 times a week. Symptoms are relieved within 10-15 minutes by using her salbutamol inhaler. No nocturnal symptoms or waking up coughing. No daily shortness of breath at rest. No recent upper respiratory tract infections.
Objective/Exam findings: Needs lung auscultation (assess for wheeze), peak expiratory flow (PEF) measurement, and inhaler technique review.
Relevant background/PMH: mild intermittent asthma (diagnosed at age 10), childhood eczema
Current medications: salbutamol 100mcg inhaler as needed (uses 2-3 times per week)
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Bronchial Asthma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Vocal cord dysfunction without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Silent chest (absent breath sounds during severe attack).
management_principles: Review and demonstrate correct MDI inhaler technique (with or without spacer)
Review a clinician-directed reliever and anti-inflammatory treatment plan before exercise; avoid relying on a short-acting bronchodilator alone as ongoing asthma treatment.
Consider step-up controller treatment based on symptom frequency, exacerbation risk, objective assessment, and current guideline-based regimen.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 32F with childhood history of asthma presents for review of exercise-induced wheezing and dyspnea. Symptoms occur 2-3 times/week, triggered by cold air/exercise. Fully relieved by SABA. No nocturnal awakenings or resting dyspnea.
reference_soap.objective: Needs lung auscultation (assess for wheeze), peak expiratory flow (PEF) measurement, and inhaler technique review.
reference_soap.assessment: Mild intermittent asthma, exercise-induced, currently well-controlled to partially controlled. DDx: exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB), vocal cord dysfunction, poor physical conditioning.
reference_soap.plan: Review inhaler technique and objective lung function where feasible, then agree a clinician-directed reliever and anti-inflammatory treatment plan and written asthma action plan. Escalate urgently for severe breathlessness, inability to speak full sentences, cyanosis, a silent chest, poor reliever response, or low oxygen saturation.

learning_objectives: Assess asthma control level using standard criteria (daytime symptoms, nighttime symptoms, reliever use, limitation of activity)
Differentiate SABA (reliever) and ICS (preventer) inhaler roles clearly to the patient
Describe and demonstrate correct inhaler technique in simple, step-by-step English
Reassure the patient and create a practical asthma action plan for exercise

teaching.one_liner: Chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by variable expiratory airflow limitation and bronchial hyperresponsiveness.
red_flags: Silent chest (absent breath sounds during severe attack)
Pulsus paradoxus, inability to speak full sentences, or poor response to reliever therapy
Hypoxemia, cyanosis, or rapidly worsening breathlessness

must_ask.say: Do you hear a high-pitched whistling sound when you breathe out or feel chest tightness?
Are your coughing and wheezing attacks worse late at night or early in the morning?
Do cold air, exercise, pollen, dust mites, or pet dander trigger your breathlessness?
Do you or your family members have allergic rhinitis, hay fever, or eczema?
How quickly does your blue rescue inhaler open up your chest during an attack?

history.answer: I've been getting short of breath and hearing a wheezing sound whenever I go running outside.
It started about a month ago when the weather turned cold, and it only happens while I'm exercising.
I can walk normally and climb stairs without any trouble, but running for more than ten minutes makes my chest tight and breathless.
It comes on during outdoor runs about two to three times a week, lasts while I run, and I feel completely normal in between.
Running outdoors in the cold air brings it on every time, especially when I push myself faster.
Whenever I stop running and take one or two puffs of my blue salbutamol inhaler, my breathing clears up completely in ten to fifteen minutes.
Yes, I hear a whistling sound when I breathe out, and my chest feels uncomfortably tight.
I get a dry cough during and right after running, but I do not cough up any mucus or phlegm.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, sore throat, or recent cold symptoms.
No, I sleep soundly through the night and never wake up coughing or feeling breathless.
No, I can lie completely flat on one pillow without any trouble breathing.
No, I don't have any sharp or squeezing pain, just that tightness across my chest when I wheeze.
No, my heart doesn't flutter or race, and I haven't felt faint or dizzy.
No, I have never coughed up any blood.
No, I haven't had any swelling in my legs or feet, and my weight has remained the same.
No leg tenderness or swelling at all, and I haven't had recent surgery, long flights, or prolonged bed rest.
No, my energy is fine during the day, and I haven't noticed pale skin, dark stools, or unusual bleeding.
No, I don't feel tingling in my hands or around my mouth, though I do get a bit anxious when my breathing tightens up.
I had eczema when I was a child, and my nose gets stuffy and itchy during pollen season in the spring.
No, I don't take beta-blockers, and taking aspirin or ibuprofen has never caused breathing problems for me.
I work inside a clean office with no dust, mold, or chemical fumes, and we don't keep any pets at home.
I think my childhood asthma is acting up again because of the colder weather and the running.
I'm worried that I might have a severe attack while running alone in the park and won't be able to breathe.
I want to see if my asthma is well-controlled, whether I should start a daily preventer inhaler, and check if my inhaler technique is correct.
I was diagnosed with mild intermittent asthma when I was ten, and I had eczema as a young child.
I have never had any surgeries and I've never been admitted to a hospital.
I use a salbutamol 100 microgram inhaler as needed about two to three times a week. I don't take any other medications or supplements.
No, I don't have any allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used electronic cigarettes.
I only drink one or two glasses of wine socially on weekends, nothing more.
I work as a graphic designer and live in an apartment with a roommate.
My periods are regular every twenty-eight days, my last period was two weeks ago, and there is no possibility of pregnancy.
My mother has allergic rhinitis, but there is no family history of heart disease, early stroke, or serious lung conditions.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 72 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.7°C, oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air.
The patient is alert, comfortable at rest, and speaks in full sentences without visible respiratory distress or cyanosis.
Symmetric chest wall motion without accessory muscle use, intercostal retractions, or chest tenderness.
Resonant percussion note bilaterally throughout all lung fields.
Clear vesicular breath sounds bilaterally without wheezing, rhonchi, or crackles at rest.
Regular rhythm and normal heart sounds S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
No jugular venous distension observed at 45 degrees.
No pretibial or pedal edema bilaterally.
Both calves are symmetric and non-tender without warmth, erythema, or palpable cords.
Mild skin dryness over the flexural surfaces of the arms, with no active eczema or acute rash.
